paragraphs.text: I resisted the urge to sneak a peek at the questionnaire of the man sitting beside me at jury duty a few weeks ago. He’d been totally unknown to me a half-hour before, but now, through the accident of being summoned to serve this civic duty on the same day, he was part of my world, an object of curiosity, my neighbor for the day. Who was this 30ish man in a plaid flannel who didn’t crack a smile when the hammy lawyer released a fellow juror with the quip, “Always the bridesmaid, never the bride”? Who were any of these people who, as I had, took the day off work and stepped out of the currents of their lives to enter this fluorescent-lit parallel universe of judgment and justice?

Jury duty presents an acute instance of the makeshift community: strangers who come together for a short period, and in that time become their own little society with its own customs and laws, its own characters and gossip. These accidental communities happen all around us, all the time: the people sitting around you on the beach, fellow passengers on a flight, other fans who started queuing for concert tickets before dawn. Unlike when, say, staying in the same bed-and-breakfast or sharing a cubicle at work, socializing is not expected; but just by being present, you’re part of the play.

How quickly people go from invisible to mattering! At jury duty, the woman who works at a nonprofit and grew up in Kansas has such thoughtful answers to the lawyers’ queries: She is the most beloved of all my new neighbors. We share a smile when we’re released for lunch, the pop-up community equivalent of best friendship. And that man in the cap watching a movie on his phone: He’s breaking the no-devices rule, and we all revile him.

By afternoon, we have familiarized ourselves with routes from the metal detector to the assembly room, assembly room to bathroom: These are our neighborhood’s streets. We all know the same sleepy security guard, the no-nonsense courthouse staff; they live here too. Our outside lives become dim — do we really have jobs and spouses and full-fledged personalities? Our friends have no idea about these people to whom we’ve uttered not a word but have somehow become our confederates, no inkling of all the infrastructure we’ve erected.

Then, as quickly as this society materialized, it evaporates. Those of us who have not been empaneled are abruptly dismissed at 4:30 p.m. There is no duty keeping us here, no actual ties to unravel, so we spill out the doors and stagger back to our actual friends and neighbors. We will probably not remember one another, and isn’t there a tiny bit of grief in that? How strange to periodically take up residency in these disposable towns, to participate in their bureaucracies so intensely and then never revisit them. We return home to our established relationships, the people we’ve lived beside for years, those who know us and whom we know. How wonderful to be recognized, depended upon, to contribute to the ongoing project of building a community we hope will last.
THE LATEST NEWS
• A teacher and a father of two girls stopped the 16-year-old assailant who killed four people at an Oregon school Thursday from doing much more damage. Read how they did it.
• Officials believe the attacker, a former special ed student at the school, used a shotgun owned by his mother. Here’s what else we know about him.
• Katie Zacharia is out after only five days as White House press secretary. Her ouster follows a shaky first news conference and questions about whether she misrepresented herself as a lawyer.
• President Trump signed an executive order exempting Russia from new sanctions legislation as part of his effort to lower gas prices.
• Trump has claimed that noncitizens vote en masse, but studies show that it is so rare that it has never changed the outcome of an election. Our graphics put the frequency in perspective.
• Our reporters talked to young voters who have given up on Trump and to residents of Republican strongholds who are struggling with drug prices.

• Four congressional districts in Pennsylvania exemplify the types of seats that Democrats are aiming to flip. In the video below, our national political correspondent Shane Goldmacher explains. Click to watch.
• Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York transferred $1 million to Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate campaign in Michigan.
• Democratic candidates have out-raised Republicans, but super PACs tied to Elon Musk and Trump have kept the G.O.P. competitive.
• Some $137 million has been spent in this election cycle on A.I.-generated ads. More than 80 percent of those were by or on behalf of Republican candidates.
Around the World
• Using new drones, Russia is trying to make life in Kyiv unbearable. See what it’s like there now.
• Dozens of Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. Times reporters witnessed the attack, in which a photojournalist from The Washington Post was among the injured.
• Crime plunged in Caracas after death squads killed thousands in 2018 and 2019. Now Venezuela is investigating that blood-soaked campaign.
• Officials in France acknowledged that they failed to keep sexual offenders from working in schools.
• A campaign to unmask the former Cornell student who accused seven men of sexual assault began on X. Our reporters tracked how it evolved.
• A 19-year-old man was charged in the rape and fentanyl death of a student at the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York.
• The international authority on timekeeping voted to eliminate the leap second. The contentious measure will be replaced, a very long time from now, with a leap hour.
• Researchers claimed to have found the world’s oldest shipwreck.
• Terence Tao, one of the world’s greatest living mathematicians, is on a “war footing” about A.I. In an interview, he told us why.
THE INTERVIEW
— Bono. He and The Edge talked to David Marchese on the occasion of the 50th anniversary of U2. They also have a new album coming out. Watch or read more of their conversation here.
THE WEEK IN CULTURE
Film and TV
• Perhaps the most in-demand screening at the Cannes Film Festival this spring was 55 years old and hated when it came out. A new restoration makes its qualities clearer.
• A cringe comedian might seem an odd choice to helm a documentary about Elizabeth Holmes — until you see Nathan Fielder’s TV shows. Get caught up with our guide.
• In 2003, the Dixie Chicks took on the president. In 2006, they took on the backlash with a Grammy-winning album. Now they’re on tour celebrating that album’s 20th anniversary.
• Barbara Kingsolver and Yiyun Li are novelists who also play piano. Both just published novels about pianists. We talked to them about it.
• The act of cutting paper is one of the world’s oldest folk arts. A new generation has given it a subversive edge.
• Trained as a historian, the painter Nilima Sheikh portrays the fractures of modern India in massive scrolls. Our critic says that her first New York show is marvelous.
GAME OF THE WEEK

Ohio State vs. Indiana, college football: The Athletic’s Justin Williams called this “the biggest home game in the history of Indiana football,” and it’s not hard to see why. The No. 5-ranked Hoosiers, who spent much of the last 70 years as the Big Ten’s punching bag, are now riding an incredible 22-game winning streak that includes last season’s national championship. Yet they’re still considered the underdog against the No. 4-ranked Buckeyes, whose star wide receiver, Jeremiah Smith, has appeared nearly impossible to defend. Kickoff is today at noon Eastern. — Matthew Cullen
REAL ESTATE
The Hunt: After years of visiting her children in New York, a Colorado sculptor decided to look for a second home near Manhattan’s galleries. What did she find? Play our game.
What you get for $400,000: An Italianate brick home in Schenectady, N.Y., a bungalow in Oregon, and a farmhouse in Indiana. Which would you choose?
Jewel box: For decades, the architect Bob Ray Offenhauser built mansions for his clients. Now his own home is on the market. Check it out.
LIVING
More space: An artist in Atlanta built his own backyard studio using salvaged materials. Go inside.
Cosmetic restoration: Mask scratches, gouges and splintering on your hardwood floors with these D.I.Y. techniques.
Home gallery: Young artists in New York are using their apartments as studios to showcase and sell their work. Meet some of them.
ADVICE FROM WIRECUTTER
Surprising things you should refrigerate

Of course, your milk and poultry need to be kept cool. But the chilly darkness of your fridge can also help many common household objects last much longer. Cold temperatures can prevent an open bottle of super glue from turning rock solid or slow the aging process of unused photo film. Same goes for expensive skin care products, like vitamin C serums. Use teeth-whitening strips? The cold helps delay the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide and other active ingredients. Just make sure any nonfood items are clearly labeled, out of sight or out of reach from anyone who might not understand that they are not safe to ingest. — Maki Yazawa
